input: The adsorption of a dye from water onto activated carbon was investigated in a series of batch tests carried out at 298 K, and the results provide a useful picture of the performance that can be achieved. In each test a measured mass of carbon was brought into contact with a volume of dye solution and the mixture was agitated while samples were withdrawn over time, so that both the approach to equilibrium and the equilibrium state itself could be observed. The equilibrium data were fitted to the Langmuir model, and the fitted capacity came out at 207 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 6, which represents a substantial uptake for this class of adsorbent. The Langmuir equation described the equilibrium data closely across the range of concentrations studied, with no systematic departure at either end of the range. In the kinetic tests, an adsorbent dose of 0.7 g L-1 was used, and after 120 min the removal had reached 84% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1, leaving a residual concentration of 8 mg L-1 in solution. These results highlight the effectiveness of activated carbon for this application and suggest that the material is capable of treating dye-bearing water to a low residual level. It is important to note, however, that the Langmuir fit is reported for pH 6 only, and the capacity at other pH values was not measured, so the fitted capacity should not be extrapolated to more acidic or more alkaline conditions without further experimental work being undertaken to support such an extension of the results.
target: Adsorption of a dye from water on activated carbon was measured in batch tests at 298 K. In each test a measured mass of carbon was contacted with a volume of dye solution and the mixture was agitated while samples were withdrawn, so that the approach to equilibrium and the equilibrium state were both observed. The fitted Langmuir capacity at pH 6 is 207 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent. The Langmuir equation described the equilibrium data closely across the concentrations studied, with no systematic departure at either end of the range. At an adsorbent dose of 0.7 g L-1, removal after 120 min reached 84% of the initial dye concentration (50 mg L-1), leaving 8 mg L-1 in solution. The capacity is an equilibrium figure from the fit, and it states the uptake the carbon approaches as the residual concentration rises; the removal figure is a kinetic result at one dose and one contact time, and the two figures answer different questions. Read together, they show a carbon that takes up a large mass of dye at equilibrium and removes most of the dye from a dilute solution within the stated contact time at the stated dose. A higher dose would raise the removal at the same contact time and lower the uptake per gram; the pair of figures fixes one operating point, not a curve. The tests are batch tests: they state nothing about behaviour in a continuous column or about capacity after regeneration. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 6 only. Capacity at other pH values was not measured. Dye uptake on carbon shifts with pH through the charge on the dye and on the surface, and the capacity figure is a figure for the stated pH; at a different pH the uptake would differ, by an amount these tests do not give.
